en: The Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There were one hundred thousand followers;

and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive and had realized the state of non-arising. They had attained skillful means, wisdom, and infinite supernormal powers, transforming beings according to the times to rescue and deliver those in the three realms.
Their names were Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and other such bodhisattvas, who all gathered there like clouds.
Seven billion two hundred million devaputras were present together, all of whom were resolved upon the Mahāyāna;
the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā, each accompanied by forty-two thousand Śakras and Brahmās, all of whom yearned for the Great Way;

and the Asura kings of the four quarters—Nandopananda, Sāgara, Manasvin, Dharaṇīdhara, Anavatapta, Parvatakūṭa, Mārapramardaka, and Candrottara—these dragon kings, each followed by sixty-two thousand of their subjects.

The ghost-king Jinbi, Kuangye, Miaomaο, Pude, Shanpu, Shanchai, Puxiang, and Wuzheng—these various ghost kings, each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of their own kind, came together to the place where the Buddha was.

They all bowed their heads in prostration and took their places in order; with single-minded devotion, they set their aspirations upon the Way of the Sūtras and were parched with longing for the Dharma. With body, speech, and mind united in reverence, they paid homage to the Buddha and listened with tranquil hearts.

At that time, the king, the crown prince, the great ministers, the various officials, the elders, the householders, the people both young and old, and the devas, nāgas, and ghost kings, all together made offerings according to their respective needs and comforts.

Then, at dawn the next morning, the Buddha donned his robes and took up his alms bowl; accompanied by the great assembly and attended on both sides by devas, nāgas, and kingly spirits, he ascended into the void. Four kinds of lotus flowers fell in profusion like rain, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, all producing the eight melodic tones of the refined hymns of Śakra and Brahmā as they proceeded to King Ajātaśatru’s palace to accept his invitation.
The Buddha manifested his supernormal powers, emitting light that illuminated the ten directions; seven-jeweled lotus flowers sprang up wherever his footsteps fell.
Transformed bodhisattvas sat upon each of them, their radiant forms so distinct as to be beyond description. They circled the city seven times and uttered this eulogy:
“The Guide is supremely divine; His compassion is immeasurable.”
Using skillful means to protect sentient beings, he eliminates illness and heals all sores.
The Muni is free from attachment; his mind is tranquil and well-composed.
That Lion’s Roar, the Illuminator of the World, today desires to enter the city.
His mind already liberated, he has crossed over birth, old age, sickness, and death;
as the hosts of devas assemble, each harbors a joyful aspiration.
His heart is exceedingly firm and strong, having subdued Māra along with his retinue.
The Lion of the Śākyas, the Most Holy One, the Venerable Guide, has already arrived.
He who does not destroy the multitudes of this world—the voice of the Truly Real is difficult to encounter;
most fierce, he is able to exercise mastery, having practiced the Path for billions of kalpas.
With a mind embracing great compassion, he universally protects all beings;
today, as the Truly Awakened One, he shall enter the city of Rājagṛha.
The acts of giving he has practiced in the past are immeasurable and boundless.
With clothing, food, various treasures, and vehicles, there is no longer any limit to his giving;
bestowing upon others his beloved sons and daughters, as well as his wife and the realm itself—
now that Lion of the Śākyas desires to enter the royal palace.
In past lives, you gave hands and feet, heads, eyes, ears, and noses;
with universal benevolence, you never acted with resistance.
You were not greedy or stingy regarding precious treasures, but gathered all meritorious deeds together, giving away everything you possessed.
Because of this, the Honored One has attained entry into all-knowledge.
By constantly and diligently practicing and studying— from generosity up to ethical discipline and wisdom—
and by guarding the precepts without flaw or leakage, he is called a true man.
Having attained the precepts, illumination, and patience, and maintaining immeasurable merit, his mind is tranquil and settled; today he shall enter the city.
Having practiced diligence and liberation for hundreds of billions of kalpas, he now approaches.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, his mind has never known weariness;
with a single-pointed mind beyond restraint, he has already crossed to the other shore.
His voice transcends that of Brahmā, and today he wishes to enter the city.
The sagely, brilliant path of wisdom is boundless and immeasurable;
its limits cannot be grasped, for it is metaphorically like space.
Such is the Jewel among Men: his wisdom and virtue are inexhaustible.
By relying on the realization of all practices, he perfected the supreme, pure wisdom.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra and his hosts;
having attained the light of the non-retrogressive path, he abides forever in peace, free from sorrow and grief.
The Sage of the Path turned the wheel of Dharma; those delivered by him are beyond measure.
Today, the Lion of the Śākyas wishes to enter the city of Rājagṛha.
If there be any who give rise to the aspiration for the Path, I shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Abiding in the world until the ultimate end, possessing the thirty-two marks,
constantly giving rise to immeasurable resolve, and with utmost sincerity awakening the mind of the Way,
they immediately take refuge in the Most Victorious One and make offerings to the Sage among Men.
Desiring to sever lust, anger, and delusion, to eliminate all the defilements of worldly toil,
and to resolve to subdue all that is harmful and flawed,
you should quickly go to the Holy Honored One, the Lion of the Śākyas.
Offering various excellent provisions with a reverent mind beyond measure;
if one desires to be born in the heavens as Śakra, the Lord of Devas, or Brahmā,
one shall be known, seen, and revered by hundreds of thousands of billions of devas.
Always encountering peace and happiness, remaining in heaven without losing the proper time,
one should go to the Lion of the Śākyas to hear the words he proclaims, which are the ultimate truth.
Those who desire to emulate the Holy Emperor and rule over the cities of the four quarters—
Spontaneously the seven treasures appeared, causing me to attain noble rank;
I possessed a thousand sons endowed with every virtue, extraordinary and exceedingly valiant,
who constantly and diligently served and took refuge in the Truly Real One, the Great Honored Person.
If one desires the rank of a venerable elder, who amasses wealth and treasures,
whose livelihood is vast, who always travels with sovereign ease,
whose retinue is entirely noble and distinguished, and whose countenance is upright and exceptionally beautiful—
One should go to the Lion of the Śākyas, who is honored with excellent and precious offerings.
Those who have already attained liberation, as well as those who seek deliverance,
should all listen attentively and receive [this teaching], for the Great Sage speaks of profound stillness.
"By hearing these words of ambrosia, one becomes tranquil and free from sorrow and affliction;
the Honored Guide among men—his voice is exceedingly difficult to encounter.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, countless multitudes, hearing this sound of praise, exhortation, and instruction, were all filled with joy and resolved to attain the Way. Each carrying various flowers and diverse exquisite incenses, along with banners, pennants, precious parasols, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, they went out of the city to welcome the Buddha. They prostrated at his feet and followed behind him.

As the World-Honored One entered the city and his feet stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the earth immediately shook in six ways. Lute-like musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; the pearl bracelets of women clashed against one another, producing sound; and from above, flowers and incense fell in profusion like rain. The blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, the lame walked, the sick were healed, the insane became sane, and those who were hunched or crippled regained their full extension. Those bitten by venomous insects found the poison no longer taking effect; the naked obtained clothing, the poor obtained wealth, and flying birds and running beasts cried out together in harmony.

At that time, sentient beings possessed hearts of loving-kindness, free from lust, anger, and delusion; they extinguished arrogance, suspicion, resentment, and doubt. Facing one another with harmony and joy, they regarded each other as fathers and mothers, as elder and younger brothers, and as their own bodies or children. Each rejoiced and uttered this praise:
"The supreme among men, like the full moon, is the true guide, the lion among men."

The World-Honored One entered the city to benefit sentient beings, universally bringing peace to all who were blind or deaf, restoring their sight and hearing; those hungry or cold were satisfied and warmed, the disturbed attained composure, the poor attained wealth, and the insane and perverse attained rectitude.
The various devas above scattered rains of flowers and incense and performed manifold musical performances as an offering.

Sentient beings possessed hearts of loving-kindness and were free from the names of the three poisons; their minds were humble and joyful, and they eliminated arrogance. They regarded one another as fathers, mothers, younger brothers, and elder brothers, and like their own bodies or children, they shared a single intent in their hearts.

The World-Honored One’s Dharma-flood moistens and nourishes the ten directions equally; the multitudes of devas and humans understand that there is nothing to be hoped for. Such merit as this is difficult to measure, as his majestic virtue proclaims the Tripitaka throughout the ten directions.

At that time, in the city, there was a son of noble lineage named Pāpamjaha (Abandoner of Evil). From afar he beheld the World-Honored One, whose gait was perfectly even, whose countenance was upright and dignified, and whose majestic spiritual radiance shone forth. His faculties were tranquil and settled, serene and profoundly silent; his nature was harmonious and refined like clear, still water. He was pure within and without, like a fierce lion, the king of beasts; like the sun newly risen illuminating the morning light; like the full moon, most brilliant among the host of stars. The Buddha stood amidst the great assembly, towering and majestic, his marks and signs resplendent and vast. With a heart full of joy, he respectfully advanced to welcome the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, joined his palms in self-surrender, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha:

"I wish to hear: by practicing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva swiftly attain true and correct enlightenment as a most perfectly awakened one, and immediately, according to their own mind, accomplish a majestic and pure buddha-field?"
"Please deign to show compassion and explain this in detail.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
Bodhisattva Abandoning Evil!
You have asked about the Tathāgata’s virtue of majestic purity; this is the extraordinary practice of all these bodhisattvas.
Listen attentively!
"Listen attentively!
Contemplate well the rules of conduct.

The Bodhisattva Abandoning Evil and the entire assembly were without exception filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with single-minded reverence and solemnity, they all came forward to pay homage to the Buddha, receiving his instructions and listening.
The Buddha said:

"There is one dharma-practice by which a bodhisattva swiftly achieves true correctness as the Most Perfectly Awakened One, and from the very moment of their resolve, they bring about the adornment and purification of a buddha-field.
What is this one thing? It is as follows:"
The mind constantly feels compassion for and seeks to deliver all sentient beings, giving rise to the most true, benevolent, and harmonious mind of the Way.
What is meant by "the most true, benevolent, and harmonious mind of the Way"?
It is said: it is to give rise to the mind of the Way while not engaging in any phenomena.
What is it that he does not practice?

It is said: He does not practice the three defilements, household affairs, or various worldly gains; his resolve is set upon leaving the home life and he does not rely on the sustenance of the multitude, but follows his original vow to always honor this Dharma.
What is meant by the practice of the Dharma revered by those who have left the household life?
It is said: to cultivate correct and true conduct and to revere all dharmas.
What is meant by the correct and true nature of all dharmas?
It is said: "To discern and thoroughly understand the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana).
What are the aggregates and elements?
What is it that is thoroughly understood?"

It is said: Both conditioned and unconditioned dharmas are all the five aggregates (*skandha*). To understand that the aggregates are like an illusion and that which is attached to them is called "knowing that the aggregates are fundamentally empty. This is what is meant by being fully awakened to the fact that illusory dharmas are fundamentally quiescent.

From opposition there arises discernment; when neither the beginning nor the end is seen, there is the non-seeing of duality. Without thought and without expectation, this is the dedicated practice and observance of renunciation, accomplishing the bodhisattva path without abandoning sentient beings.

Why is this? Because having been able to discipline oneself and attained mastery over all phenomena, one then practices eloquence for the sake of all phenomena and sentient beings, yet neither attains a sentient being nor perceives any phenomena.
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!

This is the practice of a single dharma of a bodhisattva, by which one swiftly attains true reality as the most perfectly awakened one, and from the very mind, immediately accomplishes a purified buddha-field."

Upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, the Bodhisattva Abandoning Evil was filled with joy and exultation; he immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and his body ascended into the air to a height of seven *zhang* above the ground.

At that time, as the assembly witnessed this miraculous transformation, two thousand people conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, while ten thousand four thousand devas and humans were cleansed of dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

Then the Buddha smiled, and countless rays of light issued from his mouth, illuminating immeasurable worlds in the ten directions; they then circled the Buddha three times and re-entered through the crown of his head.
The worthy Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and praised the Buddha in verse:
"Traversing all dharmas through the *pāramitās*, The Most Victorious and Truly Real One guides by power;
Having fully understood the transformations of all beings, he possesses supreme wisdom— I pray only that you will proclaim the meaning of this smile."
The One Endowed with the Ten Powers has already reached back into the past, and His compassion extends forth to future karma;
He clearly perceives all matters throughout the ten directions in the present—why, for what reason now, do You manifest a smile?
He understands the conduct of sentient beings; now, like a lion, he beholds all their minds.
His wisdom is luminous and without peer; he alone proclaims the Dharma for training the multitude.
Billions upon billions of devas have gathered from afar, all joining their palms to pay homage to the Most Holy One.
We pray that you will manifest the supreme, wondrous light and voice, so that this immeasurable assembly may behold the vessel of the Dharma.
"Your perfection of wisdom is peerless in the mundane world;
you know all people and the destinations reached by their good and evil deeds.
O Great Benevolent One, for what reason do you smile now? We pray that you will explain its meaning."
One shall resolve the web of doubts for the multitude and universally proclaim the most honored Dharma.
Now this great assembly has gathered like clouds from hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas for the sake of the Dharma; all the bhikṣus remain silent.
With increased reverence, they performed offerings, accompanied by the sounds of hundreds of thousands of musical instruments;
practicing with a tranquil mind, they listened, saying: "We only pray that you will resolve our many doubts.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this Bodhisattva Abandoning Evil dwelling in mid-air?
He replied, "I have seen him."
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

This Bodhisattva Pratyākhyānapāpa shall, after six million two hundred thousand kalpas, attain Buddhahood, with the name Śāntanirvāṇasvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world shall be named Kṣema, and his kalpa shall be named Vītarava.”
That land shall be as the World of Wondrous Joy of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; its meritorious adornments and purity shall be equal, without any difference.

Having praised this, the Buddha proceeded to the palace of King Ajātaśatru. The king, his queen, the crown prince, and the hundred officials welcomed the Buddha with flowers, incense, music, and joy; they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand behind him.
The Buddha entered and took his seat; the assembly of Bodhisattvas and holy ones each sat in their respective positions according to their order as usual.
Observing that they were seated and settled in profound stillness and silence, the King, together with the Queen and the Crown Prince, personally served them a hundred varieties of offerings.

When all had finished eating and the ritual washing was completed, he further presented rare jewels and fine garments as offerings to the Buddha. Then, taking a small chair, he sat before the Buddha and, with single-minded devotion and palms joined, listened to the teachings of the Way, desiring to transform those within the inner palace and all who had gathered for the assembly.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha: “Indeed,
World-Honored One!
From what do anger, resentment, aversion, and envy arise?
From where does that foolish ignorance come?
By what is wisdom extinguished?
The Buddha told the king:
"From the notion of 'self' arise anger, resentment, aversion, and envy; dwelling in self-conceit gives rise to delusion; failing to distinguish the true reality is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
To see and follow the true reality is wisdom (*prajñā*); just as light dispels darkness, so too does wisdom eliminate all evils, and seeing and following the true reality is likewise."
The King addressed him again, saying:
"I wish to see the correct and follow the truth; I pray that you will explain it for me.
The Buddha said to the Great King:

“The Dharma is fundamentally empty and does not arise from the mind to take form; understanding that the mind has no locus, there is neither coming nor going. To realize that all is empty is to see correctly; seeing correctly without wavering is called following the truth. To possess such complete understanding is called realization.”
When the king heard the Buddha’s words, which accorded with his mind and were taught as a Dharma discourse, he was filled with joy and delight, and wholesome thoughts arose within him.
He then exclaimed: “Excellent!
World-Honored One!”

This is most unprecedented; this is indeed the excellent teaching of the Tathāgata. Even if my life were to end this very moment, my mind would not be confused or distracted, and I would surely be able to uphold it.

The Buddha rose from his seat and, together with the great assembly, immediately returned to Vulture Peak Mountain. He commanded the attendants to arrange the various seats and invited all those gathered to take their places.
At that time, Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Just now, when the Bodhisattva Abandoning Evil asked about the subtle, wondrous, and pure Buddha-land, the World-Honored One answered by briefly citing its essential meaning. Abandoning Evil immediately received the Buddha’s prediction and prostrated himself; those who heard the explanation each attained the realization of the fruit. However, those whose minds did not grasp it were all left in a state of bewilderment."

I only pray that the World-Honored One will, out of great compassion, speak further and fully expound this, so that all bodhisattvas may strengthen their practice, abide in the right path without wavering, achieve all-knowledge, and subdue the hosts of Māra; so that they may gather in those of heterodox views, extinguish all defilements, transform and convert those of wrong karma to enter the right path, abandon the stage of the Lesser Vehicle, and turn the non-retrogressive wheel; so that they may fulfill all supreme vows to benefit sentient beings, receive the power of majestic purity to attain boundless illumination, and deliver those not yet delivered and bring to completion those not yet perfected.

The sons and daughters of noble family present in this assembly now have empty hearts and delight in hearing the Dharma; they value only its detailed exposition. We pray that the moisture of the Dharma may reach future generations; therefore, out of compassion and loving-kindness, please grant your grace to the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"This Dharma is subtle, wondrous, and extraordinary; it is the work of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. It should now be proclaimed and disseminated, and is not suitable for a small assembly. It would be better to manifest auspicious signs to move the worlds of the ten directions."
Immediately, according to his thought, he emitted light from the pores of his body, which universally illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.

The Buddhas of the ten directions each dispatched Bodhisattvas—possessing immeasurable spiritual wisdom, subtle and profound insight—who were each accompanied by assemblies of ten billion Bodhisattvas. All manifested supernatural transformations as they entered the Sahā world to behold the Buddha Śākyamuni, attend upon him, and pay their respects. Bowing their heads at the Buddha’s feet, they each declared:

"We have beheld the auspicious omen of the Buddha’s light and have been graced with your reception. Relying upon the four immeasurables, we have listened to and received your discourse on the Dharma. Our Buddha in our own land has asked us:"

"Why have you all come to the Sahā world? In that land of endurance, the five heinous crimes prevail; it is rigid, stubborn, and corrupt. There, greed, envy, lust, jealousy, abuse, and cursing abound; the hearts of its inhabitants are full of the poison of anger, and they injure one another. They are coarse, wild, perverse, and arrogant, difficult to transform. Do not go to the Sahā world and bring deep exhaustion and defilement upon yourselves."
We all once again addressed him, saying:
"We are capable and able to come to this Sahā world; even if we should encounter various afflictions, harms, being burned by fire, or cut by knives, we shall never harbor a sense of regret."

"The World-Honored One and all the noble beings are able to labor with humility and endure the instruction of sentient beings; we wish to joyfully pay them homage, attend upon them, and receive the profound sutras.
My Buddha of the native land then sent me to listen, and further commanded me, saying:
"Go, son of good family!"

Following your intention and acting in accordance with the time, firmly maintain your own mind and be careful not to become lax or doubtful; the practice of hundreds of thousands of kalpas in my own land is not equal to a single day of diligent perseverance in this world.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!

We would not consider it far to traverse worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so that we might hear the World-Honored One preach the Sūtra on Adorned Purity, as well as the essential discourses and expositions of the various Righteous Beings."
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and approached the Buddha, praising him in verse:
"Your immeasurable majesty and virtue are heard throughout the ten directions; Your light shines upon worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, above and below.
No sentient being is able to fully extol you; The noble wisdom of the Sage among men is inconceivable."
In worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, great assemblies of Bodhisattvas gather for the Dharma;
while they joyfully practice the Way and dwell with reverence, only the Honored One among Men proclaims the instructions of the Dharma.
The World-Honored One’s fame pervades the ten directions; his precepts, samādhi, and wisdom are ablaze.
His majestic deportment is unshakable like a lion, shining like the sun illuminating the void.

The devas, nāga kings, and spirits, as well as the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and the laymen and laywomen with palms joined in reverence, dwell here in compassion; pray, abide in peace and proclaim only the Dharma.
Knowing the past and what is yet to come, Discerning and clearly understanding the present,
For the sake of those beings who ought to be delivered, He uses the Vinaya to transform them and resolve their doubts.
How does a bodhisattva establish their practice, such that their land is adorned, purified, and illuminated by light?
By what cause do they fulfill all great vows?
O Supreme among Men, please proclaim this meaning.
For what reason are these free from greed and envy?
What is meant by the precepts being unviolated?
By what means do they cultivate diligent practice for the sake of the assembly?
Out of compassion for the masses of beings, you have practiced mercy;
from what source have you followed this path for countless eons? Through diligence, your power has become supreme;
with wisdom untiring, you are liberated in the unconditioned (*asamskrta*), delivering sentient beings from the afflictions of their toil and suffering.
With a mind pure and settled, always in single-minded concentration, Practicing the gates of liberation and abiding in meditative reflection,
Cultivating non-attachment like a lotus flower— How does one establish such practice to extinguish desire?
By what means do you practice these profound and wondrous deeds?
By what cause do you resolve to follow the Dharma that transcends the world?
For what reason do you subdue Māra and his hosts, and having subdued and transformed them, attain Buddhahood?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying:

“Prepare the high seat for the Dharma; the Tathāgata shall now, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten directions, extensively expound the Dharma-scripture on the ancient nature of harmony, the meritorious adornments and purity of Buddha-lands, and the vows and practices.”
Maitreya received the instruction and immediately thought to himself:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata commanded me to provide a seat,
rather than Ānanda, Maudgalyāyana, or the others?"
Mañjuśrī, knowing immediately what was in Maitreya’s mind, replied to him:

"You should know that when the Tathāgata has had you arrange these seats and preach this Dharma, it is not something that śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are able to receive and uphold; this Dharma is proclaimed solely for the sake of bodhisattvas."

At that time, Maitreya immediately entered the samādhi of "Just as It Is" (yathāvat) and prepared a seat for the Buddha four million li high, adorned with countless jewels and spread with celestial silken hangings; the radiance of the seat illuminated this trichiliocosm.
The Buddha rose and ascended the seat, and the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Śāriputra:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills their aspirations."
What are the four? First, his disposition is benevolent and harmonious.
Second, he feels compassion for all sentient beings.
The third is to be diligent and untiring.
The fourth is to maintain constant tranquility of mind and associate with virtuous friends.
These are the four dharmas by which one fulfills their aspirations.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There is another single dharma by which a bodhisattva does not lose their vow.
What is this one? It is as follows:”

Thereupon, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should study the emulation of the past lives and original practices of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya when he was practicing the bodhisattva path. He should resolve to leave the household life and delight in the conduct of a śramaṇa; in every birth throughout his lifetimes, he shall not violate his original vow, thereby advancing until he attains the title of Tathāgata, the Unarisen. This is the foremost utility of the bodhisattva: by renouncing the household, one attains ten virtues.
First, one is free from the state of greed and negligence.
Second, they always delight in dwelling in seclusion and do not practice amidst the clamor and bustle.
Third, they constantly uphold the practices of the Buddha and abandon trivialities.
Fourth, they cast aside the darkness of ignorance and all unbeneficial dharmas.
Fifth, not longing for wife, children, home, or the bonds of affection;
sixth, relinquishing the afflictions of the evil realms and unrighteousness;
seventh, embracing the blissful and virtuous abodes of the heavens.
Eighth, they never fail or lose the fundamental virtues of their past lives.
Ninth, the devas love and respect them, constantly longing to attend and protect them.
Tenth, the dragon kings and spirit lords always guard and defend them.
These are the ten virtues.

If there is a bodhisattva who does not abandon the Mahāyāna and aspires to deliver sentient beings, they should always pursue the practice of leaving the household life. This is the first dharma by which one does not lose their vow; wherever they go according to their will, whatever Buddha-land they reach, it shall immediately be realized as a pure and adorned Buddha-field. This is the foremost beneficial gain for a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are two further dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not abandon their vow.
What are these two?

First, one does not delight in the Lesser Vehicle nor study its practices, nor engage in its affairs; rather, one vows to deliver those who follow it, and does not preach its doctrines to teach and transform others.
The second is to constantly exhort sentient beings toward the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, causing them to accomplish the Buddha-dharma.
These are the two dharmas.
If one diligently and correctly instructs others with equanimity and without weariness, one will then attain and receive the ten meritorious states of virtue.
What are the ten? First, the buddha-field is comprised of those who do not study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Second, it is exclusively filled with assemblies of noble bodhisattvas.
Third, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly mindfully protect them.
Fourth, they are seen and praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, who extol their merits and preach the Dharma to them face-to-face.
Fifth, they give rise to a subtle and wondrous mind, constantly practicing what is correct and true.
Sixth, they do not aspire to the positions of Śakra, Brahmā, or the Worldly Kings, but their minds are always diligent, with their will fixed upon the Right Path.
Seventh, if born among humans, one becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who governs the four continents and guides them through the Way.
Eighth, in whatever place one is born, one does not contravene the work of the Way and constantly beholds the Buddhas, the Unsurpassed, Right, and True.
Ninth, they are loved and respected by all devas and human beings.
Tenth, they receive incalculable and immeasurable merit.
These are the ten points.

Why is this? Even if one were able to transform and deliver all sentient beings in a single Buddha-field, causing them all to attain the realization of the fruit of non-attachment, it would not equal a Bodhisattva, in the mere twinkling of an eye, exhorting and transforming a single person to resolve upon supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment; how much more so when the merits of ten such realms are wondrous and profound, being able to take whichever land one desires and immediately accomplishing the virtue of its adornment and purity according to one's wish.
"These are the two dharmas that do not contradict one's original vow.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not lose their vow and is able to fully possess the merit that adorns and purifies a buddha-field."
What are these three?
First, to delight in dwelling in seclusion and to cultivate a mind of tranquility and stillness.
Second, to always diligently and reverently guard the prohibitions and precepts, never allowing them to be deficient or omitted.
The third is: always bestowing the gift of Dharma with compassion, without expectation of clothing or food.
These are the three dharmas for firmly protecting the prohibitions and practicing the bodhisattva precepts.
By means of this, one immediately attains the ten fearlessnesses:
First, they are able to protect their observance of the precepts when entering cities and towns, and even when arriving at villages, their minds remain free from hesitation.
Second, when in assemblies, they are courageous and resolute in preaching the Dharma.
Third, when entering among the assembly for a meal, one has no fear.
Fourth, when preaching or reciting verses while at home, the mind is free from apprehension.
Fifth, even when entering a vihāra, one likewise has nothing to fear.
Sixth, dwelling among the noble assembly, one harbors no cowardice or weakness.
Seventh, in speech and discourse, one does not act out of fear.
Eighth, when approaching to serve one's teachers and preceptors, one is reverent and diligent, without arrogance, and free from dread of transgression.
Ninth, when speaking, one should always maintain a heart of compassion, with no fear of evil.
Tenth, when receiving clothing, food, bedding, or medicine, one should do so without any sense of difficulty.
These are the ten. Furthermore, by adding another ten matters, one then fully accomplishes the adornment and purification. What are these ten?
First, not fearing evil karma;
second, not craving one's kinsmen; third, not seeking fame.
Fourth, not to covet family lineage;
fifth, not to be envious of noble birth;
sixth, to always know contentment and moderation.
Seventh, they know the proper measure regarding food, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for treating illness.
Eighth, although they dwell at home, they praise and expound upon the Dharma.
Ninth, various devas come to them to pay homage, prostrate, and attend upon them.
Tenth, one never entertains thoughts that are improper; the mind constantly recollects the Buddha with joyful and focused diligence, having no concern for food or clothing.
This is how one fully accomplishes the adornment and purification of a Buddha-land.
Furthermore, there are ten matters by which one receives virtue and renown. What are these ten?
The first is: to abandon worldly assemblies and not long for causal conditions.
The second is to constantly practice dwelling in seclusion and not think of cities or towns.
The third is to keep the mind fixed on meditative reflection and be free from deviant thoughts.
The fourth is not to set one's will upon the midst of many affairs and clamorous distractions.
Fifth, the mind constantly recollects the Buddha without any other thoughts.
Sixth, one does not abandon physical well-being for the sake of causing harm.
Seventh, one purely cultivates the Brahma-faring without ever encountering obstacles.
Eighth, one attains samādhi through even minor matters.
Ninth, upon hearing the essential and sublime phrases of the explained meanings, one recognizes and remembers them without loss.
Tenth, according to the meaning and ultimate purpose of the sūtras as heard, one is able to explain them for others.
"These are the ten dharmas.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one does not lose one's vows."
What are the four?
First, the bodhisattva’s actions and speech are in accord with one another.
Second, he abandons self-conceit.
The third is to abandon greed and envy.
The fourth is to feel joy on behalf of others when seeing them at peace.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters of the most sincere and true teaching. What are these four?
First, in whatever place one is born, one’s mouth is always pure and the breath has the fragrance of the utpala lotus.
Second, their eloquence and wisdom in speech shall be without deficiency or omission.
Third, all devas and worldlings shall hold them in trust and faith.
Fourth, they shall not lose their excellent voice and will surely obtain the voice of a Buddha.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four further dharmas that constitute training and instruction. What are these four?
First, one is not reborn in the three miserable realms and harbors no hatred.
Second, regarding what is studied, one does not long for the ninety-six kinds of heterodox views that lead to delusion.
Third, enemies and evil associates find no opportunity to cause harm.
The fourth is that they are universally honored with prostrations by both the heavens and the world.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four dharmas for the dissemination of instruction.
What are the four? First, not abandoning the mind of giving, bestowing gifts with compassion when grain and rice become scarce and expensive.
Second, not coveting worldly glory or one's own wealth and possessions.
The third is to go and pay homage to those who observe the prohibitive precepts.
The fourth is that if one practices giving, one harbors no greed or envy. These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that can gladden the hearts of others and lead them to know contentment. What are these four?
First: "These sentient beings are as my own; I shall bring peace to them."

Second, these people covet wealth and rely upon their own physical strength as if it were peerless; yet the Bodhisattva adds compassion and bestows upon them what brings peace. One should reckon that such wealth and undertakings are not one's true companions, for they are constantly feared to be seized by the five aggregates without end.

Third, even if one possesses abundant wealth and treasures, many wives and children, and a vast retinue of kinsmen, one does not take pleasure in them nor become attached to one’s own country, let alone harbor expectations toward others among sentient beings.
The fourth is: to never seek wealth that is not earned through one's own labor while living among the laity.
These are the four dharmas.
When a bodhisattva practices these, they do not fail to fulfill their vow to adorn and purify a buddha-field.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which one does not lose what has been vowed. What are these five?”
First, to always delight in the sutras and the Dharma, and diligently seek the meaning of the Way;
second, to know the births, deaths, and transmigrations throughout countless eons;
third, through hearing the sutras and the Dharma, to accomplish meritorious virtues in accordance with the practices of all Buddhas.

The fourth is that whenever one hears a sutra from others, one should inquire about its meaning in every instance, establishing what practices to cultivate so as to achieve fulfillment and rapid accomplishment.
The fifth is that if one hears the Dharma of the sutras, one is able to practice and uphold it immediately.
"These are the five dharmas by which one does not fail to fulfill one's vow to adorn and purify a Buddha-field.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas by which one does not fail to fulfill one's vow."
What are the six?

First, they delight in practicing generosity with a mind free from stinginess or envy; they give their own bodies without begrudging even their lives, and they have no attachment to their wives, children, or retinues, harboring no expectations or desires for anything in return.

Second, when a bodhisattva is at home or traveling abroad for study, they would rather lose their life than violate the prohibitive precepts; they carefully guard the ever-abiding pure conduct (brahmacarya) and inspire and assist sentient beings by exhorting them toward the precepts.

Third, knowing that the body is a mere borrowing and that all phenomena are like illusions, one remains steadfastly established in the power of patience so that no adversities arise; even if one encounters poison, harm, the infliction of punishments such as swords and staves, or the afflictions of foul abuse, curses, and grief, one never gives rise to a thought of resentment.

The fourth is: to practice with diligence and a mind free from attachment, deeply contemplating impermanence as if one’s head were on fire; never being indolent or negligent whether walking, standing, lying down, or awake; and not retreating even if fire were to burn one's body and mind.

Fifth: To concentrate the mind and maintain tranquil stillness without other thoughts; to enter the silence of non-arising so that conceptualizations do not arise, the mind being like extinguished ashes and the body like withered wood.

Sixth, seeing what is correct and following the truths to eliminate the false and deceptive; understanding that the three realms are like echoes and illusions; realizing that phenomena have no permanent names, being like the form of the moon reflected in water; and out of compassion for all, exhorting and instructing sentient beings.
"These are the six dharmas by which one's wishes are immediately fulfilled, and one becomes fully endowed with merit to adorn and purify a Buddha-land.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are seven dharmas by which one does not fail in one's vows."
What are the seven?
First, to practice giving with all that one possesses, yet to have no expectation of gain from what is given.
Second, to uphold the precepts without deficiency, yet not to dwell on that which is prohibited.
Third, to exhort sentient beings toward the patience of non-arising dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Fourth, through diligent practice, to attain the state where body and mind are no longer grasped.
Fifth, to achieve meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by gathering the mind in single-minded mindfulness.
Sixth, to be fully endowed with wisdom and harbor no expectations.
Seventh, to constantly resolve upon mindfulness of the Buddha and relinquish all worldly hopes.
These are the seven dharmas by which one’s practice becomes complete and the Buddha-land is purified.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are eight dharmas by which one does not lose one's vows.
What are these eight?"
First, that which is proclaimed does not consist of speech that is without benefit.
Second, one uses the practice of giving as an adornment.
Third, the mind is gentle and supple, free from coarseness or wildness.
Fourth, to revere the Dharma Master without harboring any contempt or arrogance;
fifth, to constantly practice humility and deference, lowering one's mind to accord with the assembly;
sixth, to be pure in nature and conduct, free from any defilement.
Seventh, if one does not uphold the precepts, one understands the matter of karmic retribution.
Eighth, one does not harm one's own conduct nor disparage others.
These are the eight dharmas for purifying a Buddha-land.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Furthermore, there are nine dharmas by which one does not lose what has been vowed. What are these nine?
First, one should constantly guard one's physical conduct so that it is not impaired or lost.
Second, one should be cautious in speech so that there are no lapses or omissions.
Third, one should protect the mind so that no perverse thoughts arise.
The fourth is to cast off the mind of greed and remain unattached.
The fifth is to eradicate the mind of anger so that resentment does not arise.
The sixth is to extinguish the karma of ignorance so as not to act in delusion.
Seventh, one should always practice with utmost sincerity and without deception or delusion.
Eighth, one should practice compassion with firm resolve, such that the mind does not waver or change.
Ninth, one should rely upon virtuous friends and never abandon or distance oneself from them.
"These are the nine dharmas for purifying a Buddha-field.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which one does not lose one's vow."
What are the ten? First, upon hearing of the sufferings of hell, one harbors fear in the heart and cultivates a mind of compassion.
Second, upon hearing of the sufferings of animals, one likewise feels dread and gives rise to compassion that follows the Path.
The third is: hearing of the suffering of hungry ghosts, one fears their plight and gives rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
The fourth is: hearing of the peace of the heavens, one does not rejoice but constantly arouses great pity (*mahākaruṇā*).
Fifth, hearing that among human beings the price of grain has soared and that wicked people are inflicting harm, one gives rise to compassion and benevolence.
Sixth, one thinks to oneself:
"I shall redouble my diligent effort and endure all manner of suffering, so that the Buddha-land may become immeasurably adorned and pure."
Seventh, to cause them to be free from the afflictions of the three types of suffering and various anxieties.
Eighth, to cause their buddha-field to be abundant, level, and prosperous.
Ninth, to cause the people to be peaceful and harmonious, with limitless lifespans.
Tenth: All things arise spontaneously without names or attachments, until the attainment of unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment.
These are the ten dharmas by which one's vows do not fail and the Buddha-land is adorned and purified.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva takes flowers to go before the Tathāgata or to visit a stūpa or monastery, they should form this thought:

‘May all sentient beings have minds that are supple and pure, and countenances that are harmonious and joyful; may they be like these flowers—supple and exquisite, with forms and colors that are fragrant and clean—such that all who see them are filled with joy and love them with delight.’”

I vow that when I attain Buddhahood, may my land be filled everywhere with fragrant trees and exquisite flowers; may clothing, food, drink, variegated banners, canopies, gold, silver, and precious jewels all arise spontaneously.
May the people of that land maintain pure precepts, and may their minds be supple, harmonious, and refined by nature, attaining profound *dharmakṣānti* and unsurpassed supernormal powers.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra! That which a bodhisattva does is to put others first and himself last; he keeps in mind the peace and well-being of all beings as if they were his own father or mother. When he sees others attain peace, he rejoices with them.

He makes this vow: 'When I attain Buddhahood, may all those born in my land be peaceful and harmonious, free from jealousy and doubt, and enter into tranquil meditative concentration with minds devoid of discursive thought.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva guards his speech and never commits a transgression; he does not direct improper words toward others, his speech is always in accordance with the Dharma, and he utters nothing that is not righteous.

He makes this vow: 'When I attain Buddhahood, those born in my land shall have gentle and harmonious speech, free from anything improper, and their voices shall emerge in eight qualities, refined and elegant.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva purifies the precepts of body, speech, and mind; he further exhorts others to practice his own goodness, causing them to teach one another so that it reaches all beings.

He makes this vow: 'When I attain Buddhahood, may those who are born in my land have their body, speech, and mind complete, pure, and free from outflows, and may they be endowed with supernatural powers wherever they go.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Wherever a bodhisattva travels to promote and flourish the transformative influence of the Way, they always deliver men and women through true and correct [teachings], never discoursing on the words of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

They vow that those born in their land when they attain Buddhahood shall not hear of the practices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, they shall turn the non-retrogressive wheel and reach supreme perfect enlightenment, causing pure and virtuous conduct to spread boundlessly."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are bodhisattvas who do not envy the offerings given to others nor interrupt the sustenance provided to them, but instead rejoice and share in the joy when they see others receiving offerings;
and who vow that those born in my land at the time of their buddhahood shall have no names associated with greed or envy and shall all obtain the benefits of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there are bodhisattvas who do not praise themselves, do not speak of others' shortcomings, and do not discuss the deficiencies of the Saṃgha or the bhikṣuṇīs;

and if, upon hearing or seeing others being discussed, they regard it as if they themselves had committed such offenses—may all those who vow to be born in my land when I attain Buddhahood be made pure, so that they shall never hear the name of sin."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there are bodhisattvas who seek the Way of the sutras as one thirsts for a drink, whose resolve is fixed upon the true and correct without delighting in heterodox teachings;
and who vow that when they attain Buddhahood, those born in my land shall all delight in the Way of the sutras and seek the True Dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who constantly performs music and chants praises of the Buddha’s virtues, making offerings to the Tathāgata or to stupas and images, and uses these roots of merit to encourage and assist those in training;

may it be their vow that when they attain Buddhahood, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments shall sound spontaneously without being struck, proclaiming the eightfold Dharma-sounds so that all who hear them rejoice, and they shall all develop the mind of enlightenment and attain the true and correct."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there are bodhisattvas who see sentient beings with minds wandering in negligence and restlessness, they open for them the vision of the essential path so that they may not be agitated;

they vow that those who are born in their land when they attain Buddhahood shall have no disordered will, but rather collect their mindfulness to enter meditative concentration, taking dhyāna as their sustenance, until all mental fabrications are extinguished and they all reach perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"Even if the Tathāgata were to spend the duration of an eon extolling the merits achieved by this buddha-field, he could not exhaustively describe them through metaphors; what I have now briefly set forth for you is but a rough summary."
"If there are those who hear of these virtues of the bodhisattva’s practice and, aspiring to equal them, pursue this goal without doubt, they too shall achieve such a solemn and pure buddha-field.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains perfect enlightenment and, without losing their original vow, immediately realizes it as desired."
What are the three?
First, one's aspirations are exceptionally sublime and not shared with the multitude.
Second, one's conduct is peaceful and steadfast, and free from negligence.
"The third is to practice the Dharma as it has been heard without weariness.
These are the three. Śāriputra said:
“Excellent! It is truly unprecedented!
The Tathāgata’s skillful instruction is complete with all the factors of the path, and his aspirations have been fulfilled in the adornment and purification of the Buddha-field.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
“The Tathāgata attained Buddhahood through the accumulation of long-standing practice; he did not achieve the Way through ornate rhetoric or clever speech.

Those who act with negligence deceive themselves by entering the darkness and falling into the four inversions; they are submerged in the river of birth and death, and it is difficult for them to find a way out.
If there are Bodhisattvas who hear this sutra, they should aspire to joyfully practice it and establish themselves in non-negligence; they will surely accomplish that which has been taught above.
Thereupon, within the assembly, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas rose from their seats, joined their palms in homage, and spoke with one voice:
"O World-Honored One! We..."

May we all respectfully practice according to the Buddha’s instructions, fulfilling our aspirations and attaining the Way through such conduct. May we eliminate flowery rhetoric and the artifice of negligence, and fully master the essentials of the great vows and the virtue of the precepts. We pray that all may diligently follow this instruction, adorning themselves through practice and casting off the habits of manifold defilements.

At that time, the Buddha smiled with joy; five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating the ten directions, and after circling his body three times, it re-entered through the crown of his head.
The Venerable Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what cause and condition do you smile?"
"Now that the Buddha has smiled, there must surely be a purpose behind it.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Do you see these sons of noble family making their lion's roar?"
He replied, “I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”

The Buddha said, “This son of good family shall, in future ages, attain Buddhahood throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas. He shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. His land shall be adorned and pure, just like the Western Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī); its merits and purity shall be equal without distinction, and his lifespan shall likewise be without difference.”
He asked again: "In what way are their lifespans also without distinction?
The Buddha said:
"Each shall have a lifespan of ten kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhakramavijughoṣa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for the youth Mañjuśrī, whose merits are praised and extolled by all Buddhas, how long will it be before he now attains supreme perfect enlightenment?"
The Buddha said,
"You yourself should ask Mañjuśrī about this.
Following the Buddha's instruction, he went before Mañjuśrī and asked him:
“How long, O Benevolent Honored One, will it be before you shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realize supreme perfect enlightenment? Mañjuśrī replied:
“One should ask this question thus:”
"Does your benevolence aspire to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path? Why is this so?
If I myself were one who studies the Buddha-way, I would surely ask such a question."
"If I do not seek the Way, by what cause shall I achieve supreme perfect enlightenment?
He asked again,
"Does your reverence not seek supreme perfect enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings?"
He replied: "No! Why is that? Because..."
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Even if I were to find a location for sentient beings, I would still resolve to seek the Buddha-way for their sake. Why is this so?
"Because there is no self, person, or life-span, for this reason, the body has neither aspiration nor regression.
He asked again:
"Do you, O Virtuous One, not seek the Buddha or long for the Buddha-dharma?"
He replied: "No! Why is that? Because..."

All dharmas are entirely the Buddha-dharma. If one causes all dharmas to be non-existent, such that there are no outflows and no grasping, and no conceptualization regarding causes and conditions—this is the aspiration for the Buddha-way; understanding it thus, one attains all dharmas.
Furthermore, as you asked about establishing the Buddha-dharma,
I shall answer according to your intention:
who is it that seeks this resolve?
Does one aspire to the Buddha-way through form?
Does one aspire to the Buddha-way through the fundamental purity of form?
Or does one aspire to the Buddha-way through the fact that form is fundamentally non-existent?

Form is spontaneous; form is entirely empty; form is ethereal; form is fundamentally pure; form is tranquil. Is it by means of this dharma of form that one aspires to the Buddha-way and achieves perfect enlightenment?
He replied: "No! Form does not aspire to the Way;
it is fundamentally pure and spontaneous by nature."
"Because it is empty and quiescent, all dharmas of form do not aspire to seek the Way nor achieve perfect enlightenment;
the same is true for dharmas. Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Do sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the dharmas of consciousness aspire to seek the Buddha-way?"
He replied, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
“The five aggregates and the consciousness-element do not achieve perfect enlightenment. What do you think?
Can it be said that there is a location for the external five aggregates, the self, the person, or the life-span?”
He replied, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
"In this way, I shall distinguish: by what dharmas does one who aspires to the Buddha-way achieve supreme perfect enlightenment?
He then asked Mañjuśrī: "When newly initiated bodhisattvas hear these instructions, will they not become terrified?"
Why is this? Your honorable name is that of the foremost leader of all, a heavy responsibility for the multitude;
yet now you have attained realization and proclaim the various dharmas to the bodhisattvas, without aspiring to seek the Way or achieving perfect enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī replied: “The dharma-realm is not afraid;
the ultimate limit is not fearful. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, one has no dread or difficulty.
Those who are fearful harbor sorrow and grief; those without sorrow and grief are free from the dust of defilement, and they are liberated.”

That which is liberation is non-attachment; because there is no attachment, there is no further transmigration; because there is no further transmigration, there is no further liberation. That which is not liberated comes from nowhere; because it comes from nowhere, it likewise does not go anywhere. Because it does not go anywhere, there is no aspiration; because there is no aspiration, there is no seeking; because there is no seeking, there is no regression.
Because there is no regression; if there is no regression, then one does not regress. It is empty and without non-turning, without ideation, and without aspiration.

This primordial limit is the non-regression of the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha-dharma is unconditioned and has no boundary. The Buddha-dharma is without attachment and thus has nothing upon which to rely; the Buddha-dharma is without practice and likewise without diligence, and it is without any object of practice or any instruction. All these Buddha-dharmas are merely provisional designations.

Furthermore, one calculates that the dharma of emptiness arises from nowhere, comes from nowhere, and goes nowhere; furthermore, one calculates that the Buddha-dharma does not depart from the defilements of greed, anger, and delusion. The Buddha-dharma is unstained by the conduct of defilement; it is devoid of a self, tranquil, and free from thought. Its practice is non-conceptual, inexhaustible, and unarisen; it is impartial and without deviation, such that all Buddha-dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this? Because there is no locus and no one who can practice; this is called the Buddha-dharma.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva hears this teaching and feels terror, they will swiftly attain perfect enlightenment; if they do not feel terror, they will not attain perfect enlightenment.
He asked Mañjuśrī again,
"For whom was this spoken? Mañjuśrī replied:
"That which is fearful is merely conceptual construction; because of this conceptual construction, the mind thinks to itself:
'I shall attain the state of supreme perfect enlightenment.'"
"For this reason, he gave rise to the resolve for the Way and set his mind upon perfect enlightenment.
What do you think?
Has there ever been one who attained awakening and yet remained empty?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “There is none. Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"The World-Honored One has not said that all dharmas are equal to empty space? He replied, "That is so."

Mañjuśrī spoke again: "The Way is like empty space; both are fundamentally non-existent. Empty space is like the Way, and the Way is like empty space. Between emptiness and the Way there is no duality; they cannot be distinguished."
"One who understands these things has neither anything to know, nor is it that they lack wisdom.

When Mañjuśrī spoke these words, four thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; twelve koṭis of the assembly attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; ninety-six thousand people who had not previously resolved their minds for the Path all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment; and forty-two thousand people attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
The Sutra on the Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field, Volume One;
The Sutra on the Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Lion-Gait-Thunder-Voice again asked Mañjuśrī:
"For how long must one have resolved their mind [upon awakening] before they should give rise to the bodhicitta? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Stop, son of good family!
Do not harbor such deluded thoughts."
All dharmas are fundamentally unarisen; should one say,
"I have resolved to attain the Way, and I shall practice the Way," they fall into a great false view.

Why is this? Because when one now observes the mind, it is entirely and eternally unfindable; even when the mind gives rise to the thought of enlightenment, one likewise does not observe that which gives rise to the thought of enlightenment.
"I also do not perceive where the mind of enlightenment resides; for this reason, I have not resolved to attain the mind of enlightenment.
He asked again:
"O Virtuous One!"
"Since there is nothing to be seen, for what reason do you now proclaim these verses?
Mañjuśrī replied, "That which is without anything to be seen is the equal teaching; that which has no object of perception is called the equality of words in these verses."
He asked again:
"For what reason do you say that they proceed toward equality? Mañjuśrī replied:

“Regarding what the son of good family has said, ‘equality’ means there are no distinctions; that which is equal possesses no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). There is no analogy for such equality, and the non-perception of all phenomena is itself equality.”

If one proclaims this teaching, then one proclaims the single karma; if one is serene, then karma is free from defilement. One does not preach the Dharma out of anger or resentment; one neither adheres to annihilation nor calculates permanence. There is no arising and no ceasing, no self and nothing to be grasped. There is neither elevation nor depression, neither loftiness nor meanness. Although there is something preached, it is without delusive thought and without seeking.
"O son of noble family!
If there is one who understands this Dharma and practices it, that is called 'equality.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters extensively into the Dharma, seeing neither multiplicity nor unity, that is called 'equality.'"
"That which is equanimous has no partiality; that which is without partiality is utterly pure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
"How sublime indeed is that which Mañjuśrī has spoken!
How long has it been since he first resolved his mind upon the Way?
The assembly is filled with longing and thirst for the Dharma; we pray and desire to hear it."
The Buddha said, “Son of good family!

Mañjuśrī abides in profound and wondrous patience; the deep patience he enters does not involve attaining the Way, nor does it involve attaining Buddhahood, nor does it involve attaining the mind. Because there is nothing to be attained, he does not speak of it. For how long has he set forth his mind and aroused the aspiration for the Way? Only the Buddha may now explain for you the original arousal of that mind.”

In the distant past, seven thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Ghoṣadatta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He resided in the eastern direction, seventy-two *nayuta* of Buddha-lands away from here; his world was named Suvibhakta. In that Buddha-land, he proclaimed the Way and its teachings, with a multitude of eighty-four billion *nayuta* of śrāvaka disciples, and the number of bodhisattvas was twice that.
At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Anaba, titled a Dharma King; he governed the four continents under the laws of the king and possessed the seven treasures.
At that time, the Holy King went to the presence of the Tathāgata Thunderous Resonance and made offerings with all his heart for eighty-four thousand years, attending to him according to his needs.
The King thought to himself:
"I have already accumulated immeasurable meritorious deeds; I shall not employ this mind [for mere self-benefit], but rather I shall cultivate and assist through the roots of virtue."
He further reflected:
"If I am to encourage others through virtue, what should I encourage them to seek?
Is it the status of a Heavenly Lord, a Brahma King, a Cakravartin Sage King, a Śrāvaka, or a Pratyekabuddha?"
As soon as he had formed this thought, a great voice resounded from the void above: "Great King!
Do not give rise to such base thoughts; you should instead resolve to attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path."
Upon hearing these words, the king was immediately filled with great joy.
His heart of vast compassion expanded, and his resolve for the Way did not waver. Why was this so?
Because the deva had manifested this sign to instruct him, he understood my thoughts.

At that time, King Anabha, together with a great assembly of ninety-six *koṭis* of nayutas of people, went to the Tathāgata Thunderous Resonance, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
He praised him with a verse, saying:
"I wish to ask about the supreme Dharma; you have answered me with marvelous elegance:
'How does a person in this world Attain the most transcendent excellence?'"
Making universal offerings to all, I take refuge in the Protector of the World;
with a mind free from attachment, I shall never again seek worldly assistance.
The World-Honored One perceives this: that I alone have given rise to the aspiration for tranquility.
To extensively perform offerings, how should one encourage and assist them?
One should set one's mind on the status of Śakra or Brahmā, or become a king of the four quarters;
if one seeks the state of a śrāvaka, one should aspire to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.
Just as this thought arose in me, a great voice resounded from the sky:
"O Benevolent One, be careful not to encourage an inferior mind;
for the sake of all beings, you should give rise to a sublime mind."
Revealing the intent of the Great Way, To bring benefit to the world.
Now I wish to ask the Buddha, Who is sovereign over all dharmas:
“How does one give rise to the resolve for enlightenment, So as not to lose the intent of the Way?”
Please explain this profound meaning: by what cause does one reach this state?
How is it that those who resemble me have given rise to the bodhicitta?
O Honored One among Gods, please speak; proclaim these sublime verses.
"Great King, listen for a moment; I shall proclaim the gradual instruction:
'Have compassion for all sentient beings, take delight in abiding in the root of the Dharma, and according to your pledged vows, you shall attain your destined goal.'"
I, too, in past lives, gave rise to the mind of enlightenment out of compassion for sentient beings and made this vow.
Just as I originally intended and just as my heart has conceived, [so shall it be].
Upon attaining the unshakable path of Buddhahood, you shall become a World-Honored One, a Sage supreme in tranquility.
Great King, you should strengthen your resolve and cultivate the most exalted mind;
if you practice all correct deeds, you too shall attain Buddhahood.
Upon hearing these words of instruction, the king’s mind became joyful;
throughout the entire world, he proclaimed the lion’s roar:
“Even if one were to go back to the primordial limit, and did not know the origin of birth and death, [one would still find it].”
Acting for the sake of each and every individual, as if for as many sentient beings as there are;
now having resolved upon the mind of the Way, throughout all worlds,
I universally entreat all sentient beings, so that they may not fall into poverty and destitution.
From this day forward, should you give rise to a mind of desire,
you would immediately deceive all Buddhas and the holy ones currently present throughout the ten directions.
Should you give rise to anger, resentment, or weariness, or harbor jealousy and the suffering of greed, [you would likewise deceive them].
Never having committed what is forbidden, one becomes the Honored One among men.
One should always cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), abandon desire, and cast off defilement and evil.
One should learn from all the Buddhas to harmonize one’s nature through the precepts and prohibitions.
Not by means of these four colors does one swiftly attain the perfect awakening of a Buddha;
because of the intensity of one's resolve, one should practice at the ultimate limit.
One should constantly adorn and purify the Buddha-fields, which are infinite and inconceivable.
When the name is proclaimed, it shall penetrate throughout the ten directions.
May the Sage alone bestow wisdom upon him, so that he may become a Buddha, supreme among men;
may his mind be purified, forever free from all doubt.
Constantly cultivate and purify bodily conduct, And likewise with verbal speech;
One should also purify the mind’s thoughts, So as not to commit any faults or blemishes.
Even if I were to attain Buddhahood And become the Honored One among those in the world,
By these true and correct mantras, the earth shall tremble six times.
If my words are sincere, truly authentic and not false,
let this be witnessed and proven by the proclamation of music from the void.
If one is truly without flattery or deceit, free from greed, envy, or weariness,
then by virtue of such sincerity and faith, flowers of pure intention rain down.
As soon as these words were spoken, they were proven true and not otherwise.
In billions of lands throughout the ten directions, the earth shook in six ways;
in the void above, there was music on a vast scale,
and the heavens rained down flowers of various colors, accumulating to a depth of four zhang and nine chi upon the ground.
Because that king studied this, twenty billion people proclaimed gentle and harmonious voices;
they will surely attain the supreme path of Buddhahood.
These twenty billion beings alike shall all establish themselves in the Buddha-way.
"Seeing that the King had set forth upon the Great Way, I also emulated and studied his magnificent enterprise.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Siṃhakramavijitagarjitasvara:
"Do you wish to know who the King Anaba was at that time?"
He replied, “It does not compare.
The Buddha said:

"This is none other than the present Mañjuśrī! Since he first resolved his mind upon the Way, as many eons as there are grains of dust filling Buddha-lands throughout seven thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands have passed. Having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), forty-six more eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have elapsed. During those lifetimes, he has perfected the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and accomplished the ten powers (*daśabala*). He has universally prepared all the grounds of the Buddhas' path and mastered all Buddha-dharmas. From the very beginning, he has never once given rise to a thought of generating the resolve [for awakening] again; rather, he has consistently reached the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become a Most Perfectly Awakened One (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha*).
Even I do not harbor the thought: 'How shall I achieve the state of a Most Perfectly Awakened One?'"

Those twenty billion people who, in the past, had resolved their minds on the Way under the Tathāgata Resounding Thunder were all already able to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; having realized supreme perfect enlightenment, they turned the wheel of Dharma, performed Buddha-works for the sake of all sentient beings, and have since entered parinirvāṇa.

All of them were inspired by Mañjuśrī; they have all made offerings and diligently cultivated the various practices, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), universally upholding and proclaiming the True Dharma.

At present, there is currently but one Buddha who is preaching the Dharma and has not yet entered parinirvāṇa. Forty-four *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Buddha-lands away from here, in a region of the lower direction, there is a world named *Pātāla*. Its Buddha is named Dharaṇīdhara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is currently preaching the Dharma together with an incalculable number of śrāvakas, and his lifespan is limitless.
When the Buddha had spoken this parable of the past, seven thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Siṃhagāminigarjitasvara asked Mañjuśrī, “Virtuous One, you were present at the time of the Buddhas of the past;
you possessed all dharmas, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and had already perfected the ten stages. For what reason did you not attain perfect enlightenment?”
Mañjuśrī replied, "One does not attain supreme perfect enlightenment through all the dharmas of the Buddhas of the past and those who have gone before. Why is this so?"
"This statement that attaining the Way is itself non-attainment, and that there is nothing to be reached," he said.
He asked again:
"How does one become fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma?"
He replied, “Because they are fundamentally non-existent.
He asked again:
“What is meant by ‘being fully endowed with original non-existence’? He replied:

“To be thoroughly acquainted with emptiness is to be fully endowed with original non-existence; to clearly understand the meaning of the original non-existence of both emptiness and all Buddha-dharmas, such that they are equal and without duality, and cannot be distinguished.”
He asked again:
"How does one become endowed with all dharmas? He replied:
“Only by being fully endowed with the five aggregates can one possess all that exists within the three realms and universally prepare for the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He asked again:
“How does one become fully endowed with all forms?”
He replied: "Virtuous ones, you see forms.
Are forms permanent?"
"Is it impermanent? He replied, "No."
He asked: "Are all phenomena permanent or impermanent?
Furthermore, do those five aggregates increase or decrease?"
He replied, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Therefore, son of good family!
If one neither increases nor decreases with respect to all dharmas, it is called 'being fully endowed. He said:"
"What does it mean to be 'fully endowed'? He replied:

"When one is fully equipped with the wisdom of all dharmas yet has nothing to understand, and likewise when the wisdom of suchness does not turn, only then does one no longer know the locus of deluded thoughts. Because there are no deluded thoughts, one neither constructs nor destroys. This state of neither constructing nor destroying is called equanimity."
Therefore, son of good family!
When one views all forms with equanimity, one then views all dharmas—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—in the same way; they are likewise equal and without distinction.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Siṃhagāminigarjitasvara asked Mañjuśrī, "Furthermore, observe, O Benevolent One:

since you attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), an immense, vast, and sublime period of time has elapsed. It is not as if you have attained the Way through a single arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*)."
“O Benevolent One!
How do you exhort and transform sentient beings so that they give rise to the aspiration for the Way? He replied:
“Did I not exhort sentient beings to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment?
He asked again:
“For what reason?”
He replied: "Sentient beings are unreal; sentient beings are quiescent. Because they dwell in perversion, I exhort and transform them to cause them to resolve upon the Way.
If sentient beings did not abide in perversion, there would be no Way—what then would there be to resolve upon?"
For this reason, I do not exhort sentient beings to give rise to the mind of enlightenment, nor do I transform them so that they all seek the Way.

Why is this? That which is without conceptualization is called equality. Regarding the meaning of equality, there is nothing to aspire toward or seek, nor is there any retrogression; therefore, it is named "having no destination" and "having nowhere from which it comes."
