One should contemplate birth and death as what is called equality; these phrases are empty, and in emptiness there is no seeking.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Regarding that which you asked just now:
"Since attaining the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), a vast, remote, and sublime interval has passed; it is not merely once that I have resolved, 'I shall attain Buddhahood.
Do you perceive this mind?"
"By what kind of mind does one attain Buddhahood? He replied, "No."
Why is this so? The mind is formless and cannot be seen; the Way is likewise, having neither form nor color and being likewise invisible.
That which is called the "Way" is merely a provisional designation!
"What is called 'mind' and 'the Buddha-way' are both merely provisional designations.
"Therefore, son of good family! I have proclaimed this teaching not once:

'I shall attain Buddhahood by generating the aspiration for enlightenment. Yet, there is no generation of aspiration, no arising, and no destruction. That which is without arising and without destruction is what is called 'attainment.'"
He asked again:
"What is it that is called 'the time when one says it is the time,' such that it is then said to be 'time'? He replied:

“O son of noble family! That which is called ‘time’ refers to the manifestation of equal enlightenment. That which is realized neither increases nor decreases; it never gives rise to conceptualization, nor is there anything to be extinguished. Only then is it termed ‘conforming to the time of equality. When one is free from false imaginings and realizes that all things are fundamentally non-existent and originally as they are, this is termed ‘conforming to the time of equality.’”

If one attains right view, being equal within equality and penetrating all phenomena, such that there is nothing at all to be acquired and no conceptual calculations are formed, and one does not give rise to even a single thought regarding various categories—this is what is called the time of conforming to equality.
If one realizes through bodily witness that all dharmas are such that whatever marks they possess are all merely dharma-marks, then because of understanding this, there arises attachment to the mind;
if there are no marks, then there is nothing to rely upon, and this is what is called "equanimity according with the times."
He asked again,
"What is meant by 'attainment'? Mañjuśrī replied:
"There is no 'going'!

It is called 'attainment' because it refers to the traces left by names; yet, within the three realms, there is absolutely nothing to be gone toward. This expression exists only as a provisional designation, for one who has acquired the afflictions (kleśa) cannot truly attain."
Why is this so? Because the mind has no place of abiding and this Dharma is wordless; for this reason, it cannot be attained.
Furthermore, son of good family!

To have nothing to attain is called "attainment"; to have nothing to speak of is not to attain the Dharma and thus has no place of abiding; if one does not grasp at dharmas, this is called "attainment."
Then, the Bodhisattva Siṃhagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent, excellent,
World-Honored One!”
“Only the Tathāgata can say; when Mañjuśrī attains the Way of the Buddha, what will his land be like?
The Buddha told him: “Ask Mañjuśrī about this matter.”
He immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction and asked Mañjuśrī,
“When you attain Buddhahood, what will your land be like? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Noble son! If you, virtuous one, delight in the Buddha-way, you should ask what kind of Buddha-land is attained upon becoming a Buddha. He then asked Mañjuśrī:
“O Benevolent One!
Do you not delight in the Buddha-lands? He replied:
"No," he replied.
He asked again,
"For what reason?"

He replied: "Where there is that which is enjoyed, there is desire for pleasure; where there is desire for pleasure, there is affection; where there is affection, there is grasping; if there is grasping, there is suffering and affliction; where there is suffering and affliction, there is no protection. For this reason, my body has not attained perfect enlightenment."
Why is this? Because there is nothing to be attained; if one does not attain the Way, there is consequently no joy.
Furthermore, it is as you have just said, O Virtuous One:
"What kind of land is it? Describe its origins and details.
I am unable to endure compromising my own person. Why is this so?

If there is a bodhisattva who, because of praising himself, thereby diminishes and destroys the merit, adornment, and purity of the Buddha and his land, and fails to behold the Tathāgata’s boundless treasury of Dharma face-to-face.
At that time, the Buddha addressed him, saying:
"Mañjuśrī! It is fitting that you speak now of the meritorious deeds and the pure adornment of your own buddha-field; by what vows and aspirations do you intend to accomplish this?"
The Tathāgata has granted his approval.
There may be other bodhisattvas who, having heard your exposition of these vows from you, will resolve their minds accordingly and fulfill this practice. Mañjuśrī replied:
"So be it! We dare not disobey your instructions.
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"I shall now proclaim it solely by receiving your sacred decree.
If sons of good family or daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way will listen together, having heard it, they shall fully attain the practice of these aspirations."
At that moment, the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shook in six ways.
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
My original vow is as the Buddha has spoken.

For seven thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have practiced the bodhisattva path; yet I did not complete the site of enlightenment nor attain perfect awakening. With the eye of the Way piercing through and its light beholding the ten directions, I saw all Buddhas universally exhorting and transforming all sentient beings so that they might all achieve the Buddha-way. My mind remained firm and steadfast as I transformed them all, encouraging and assisting them through giving, morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—all of which were transformations brought about by my own person.
"Indeed, O Great Sage!

Now, observing the ten directions with my unimpeded, pure, and clear eyes, I see that all Buddhas have exhorted and assisted in establishing the unsurpassed, right, and true path; these matters are all accomplished, and thus I shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become the Most Perfectly Awakened One."
"Although he has spoken these words, he nevertheless continues to establish himself as not yet attaining perfect enlightenment; only when his vows are fully fulfilled shall he become a Buddha.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas in the assembly each thought to themselves:
"How many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, has Mañjuśrī encountered throughout his past and present lives?"
At that time, the Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattvas, addressed the Bodhisattva Lion-Gait Thunder-Sound, saying:
"It is just as if, son of good family!

Suppose there were a man who appeared in the world, who took this trichiliocosm—the Buddha-field of three thousand great thousand worlds—and filled it with dust; having taken that dust, he broke it apart, crushing each individual particle until each was as small as the number of dust particles that fill a single Buddha-field.
"Noble son! What do you think?
Is there anyone who could possibly know the number of these particles?"
He replied: "There is no one who can know it,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:
"Suppose, son of good family!
One were able to fully comprehend and know the number of buddha-fields as numerous as atoms—this would not even be worth mentioning."

Mañjuśrī, with his clear vision, beholds the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; he has seen more than hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, billions, and trillions of times the number of lands as fine as motes of dust—immeasurable, boundless, and beyond the limit of kalpas numbering in the millions and billions. Only when such vows are fulfilled does he attain perfect enlightenment.

Even if Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled on all sides in the ten directions with Bodhi trees, and beneath each tree there were seated Bodhisattvas who, in a single moment, all simultaneously attained the path of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment and reached Supreme Awakening—when they were about to enter Parinirvāṇa, it would not be necessary for them to establish a Bodhi tree or a site of enlightenment, yet they would universally act for the sake of all beings.
Furthermore, he shall pass beyond incalculable Buddha-lands in the ten directions, transforming sentient beings and preaching the Dharma to bring them across.

His vows were so lofty that he has now reached this Buddha-land and attained the Way of the Buddha. Within this land, there shall be no names for Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it shall consist purely of Bodhisattvas. He shall eliminate the hardships of weariness, exhaustion, and resentment, and purely cultivate the Brahma-conduct throughout the entire Buddha-field. Therein, even the name of "woman" shall not be heard; all Bodhisattvas shall be born by transformation, clad in Dharma robes and sitting in the full lotus posture. This Buddha-land shall be solemn and pure, consisting solely of Bodhisattvas, flourishing and magnificent, with the Small Vehicle teachings entirely removed.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Siṃhakramagarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“At the time you attain Buddhahood, what will your title be?
The Buddha said:
"He is named Samantadarśin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is he called 'Universal Manifestation'?

It is because the merits of that Buddha manifest throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions. All who behold Samantadarśin Tathāgata, or perceive his radiance, shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression and achieve supreme, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, whether now or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who hear the name of the future Buddha Samantadarśin shall likewise receive the prediction of their enlightenment and subsequently achieve supreme, perfect enlightenment—except for those who have entered the state of cessation and attained the fruit of the path."
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

When I have attained Buddhahood according to my vow, for those born in my land, may they be free from the perception of hunger, thirst, or the need for food and drink. May all varieties of flavors and delicacies naturally fill their bowls, resting in their right palms; as soon as they are in the palms, the thought shall arise within their hearts:”

"It is improper to eat before first making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and to those who are impoverished, distressed, begging, or lowly; one should first satisfy all others and only then eat."

Then, in accordance with his thoughts, he became fully endowed with supernormal powers; wherever he went, there was no obstruction, and he traveled as swiftly as he intended, immediately reaching the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas and descend universally upon all sentient beings.

The same applies to precious robes and Dharma garments: first they are offered to the Buddhas, then to those who are honored; even the most impoverished and lowly are first made secure, so that they are free from the eight difficulties and the afflictions of various sufferings.

Their speech is pleasing to the mind, and they do not hear harsh words; their learning is free from the sounds of prohibitions, precepts, right, and wrong. There is neither noble nor base, neither rich nor poor; all those born in my country are of one and the same kind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhakramagarjitasvara came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In that land at that time, were there no names or designations?
The Buddha said:
“As his original vow has been fulfilled according to his aspiration, the world shall be named Free from Dust and Defilement in Mind.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“In which direction is it located?”

The Buddha said: "It lies in the southern direction, at the very furthest edge of this Sahā world-system. This buddha-field is composed of various wondrous jewels, maṇi-gems, and bright pearls; it has never before been seen or heard of by anyone throughout the ten directions. Exquisite treasures and myriad jewels are distributed and manifest everywhere, never decaying or diminishing. Whatever jewels a bodhisattva desires to have that land transform into, they are accomplished as soon as they are thought of, according to whatever jewel he intends to create."

All manner of exquisite incenses and flowers are provided at will; furthermore, there is neither sun nor moon, nor light and darkness, nor day and night. If the radiance from the bodies of the Bodhisattvas shines upon them, it accords with their wishes; only the opening and closing of the flowers distinguish day from night. There is no cold or heat, nor the affairs of old age, sickness, death, or birth. One merely practices the path of a Bodhisattva and immediately attains Perfect Enlightenment. Even when going to other lands, there are no different karmic activities; whether in the heavens or the world, all practice as Bodhisattvas. When facing the end of life and passing away, they all attain Perfect Enlightenment; there is no such thing as final death or intermediate parinirvāṇa.

Within the void, the sounds of musical performances and harmonious lamentations were not seen; yet these sounds arose spontaneously, without proclaiming words of desire, but constantly producing the sounds of the Buddha-dharma, the Six Pāramitās, and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Sūtras. According to their inclinations, they heard the sounds of the sūtra-dharma; as soon as they thought of it, they understood, and all gave rise to right awakening. Upon seeing the Buddha, their doubts were extinguished; upon hearing the sūtra, they attained comprehension and penetration.
At that time, there were countless multitudes of bodhisattvas in the assembly who simultaneously raised their voices and proclaimed a great sound.
The Buddha, hearing this cry which was most appropriate for the occasion, spoke the name "Universally Manifesting Without Contradiction to the Way of Teaching":

"If any sentient beings hear the name 'Universally Manifesting,' they shall obtain swift benefit and boundless celebration; how much more so for those born in that land who behold Universally Manifesting and encounter his divine transformations, his Dharma principles, and his conduct."

If there are those who hear this decisive teaching, they shall be as if seeing the Buddha and hearing the sutra; they will enter it into the treasury of their hearts and never forget it. Merely to attain the hearing of Mañjuśrī’s name and his virtues as a Buddha—how majestic they are! How much more so, then, to behold him with one's own eyes.
At that time, the Buddha addressed these bodhisattvas, saying:

"If there were someone who, upon hearing the names, titles, merits, and praises of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, benefited sentient beings and transformed them for their deliverance, they would not equal Mañjuśrī, who in each and every kalpa transforms and guides sentient beings so that they dwell forever in peace and freedom from affliction. How much more so for one who encounters the Tathāgata Samantadarśin? His celebration is beyond compare, exactly as you have said."

Thereupon, when the assembly heard the Buddha’s praise of these bodhisattvas, ten trillion devas, kings, and worldly people within the gathering simultaneously prostrated themselves in homage to Mañjuśrī and spoke with one voice:
“We now take refuge in the Tathāgata Samantadarśin.”

As soon as they had completed their taking of refuge, eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of beings all resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; furthermore, immeasurable others accumulated the roots of manifold virtues and established themselves in non-retrogression.
Then Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now, I vow that these incalculable and immeasurable Buddha-lands, with their meritorious adornments and purities visible to the eye, shall—by virtue of this auspicious response resulting from my vow—all be merged together into a single Buddha-land. Setting aside the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even if I were to spend eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges praising the meritorious adornments and purities of those lands during the mere moment of conceiving this thought, they would be limitless and bottomless; yet my own vow surpasses even that. There is no one capable of ultimately verifying it, for only the Buddha, with his subtle and clear wisdom, knows me alone."
The Buddha said: “Excellent! It is truly as you have said;
the Tathāgata’s supernormal wisdom and the threefold penetration are unimpeded, and it is indeed so, indeed so, without any difference.”
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas within the gathering again thought to themselves:

"As the Buddha has praised the merit and purity of Mañjuśrī’s buddha-field when he attains enlightenment, how does it compare to the purity and adornment of the Western World of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) of Amitāyus Buddha?"
At that time, the Buddha, knowing the thoughts of all the bodhisattvas, addressed the Bodhisattva Lion-Gait Thunder-Sound:
"If you wish to know the majestic purity of the merits of the Buddha Amitāyus in the Western World of Peaceful Nurturing, it is difficult even for Mañjuśrī to provide a metaphor for it!"

To speak by way of analogy: suppose one were to take a single hair and break it into a hundred parts; if one were to take a single drop of seawater with one such part of hair, the Buddha Amitāyus would be like that single drop of water from the hair-part, whereas Mañjuśrī’s attainment of Buddhahood is vast as the ocean, majestic and boundless, inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhakramavikrāntaghoṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Has there ever been, in other directions, the land of a Tathāgata as adorned and pure as this?"
The Buddha said: "There is!

To the east, beyond as many worlds as there are grains of sand in ten billion Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Transcendent Establishment of Vows. Its Buddha is named Samantaprakāśasamyaksambuddha-vimalatejorājā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas, he is preaching the Dharma-sūtra. He has been manifesting and teaching since kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and the lifespan of that Buddha is likewise without limit. It is equal in its majestic purity to the Land of Universal Manifestation; therein dwell four bodhisattvas who have donned the armor of great vows and attained the inconceivable."
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"I only pray that you will take pity on us and proclaim what has not yet been heard, fully describing the pure adornments of the land of the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Constantly Illumining Virtue Ocean King, as well as the names of those four bodhisattvas."
"In which direction does he dwell, and in which Buddha-field does he roam, that he is so fully endowed with pure virtues as to be able to possess such a place?
The Buddha said, "The foremost bodhisattva is named Prabhāśrī; he roams in the eastern Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Aśokaśiras."
The second bodhisattva is named Prajñottara, residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Prajñārāja in the south;
the third bodhisattva is named Śāntendriya, residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Jñānaskandha in the west;
the fourth bodhisattva is named Manasvī, residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śṛṅkhaladhara in the north.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi known as "Universal Manifestation of Adorned Purity" (Sarvavyūha-viśuddhi-saṃdarśana). Instantly, he beheld the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata King of the Ocean of Constantly Illuminating Universal Virtue in the eastern direction, as well as the meritorious adornments and purity of its bodhisattvas—things never before seen or heard since antiquity—as clearly as if one were looking at a precious jewel in the palm of one's hand, no different from the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Universal Manifestation.
The entire assembly beheld this and was without exception filled with joy; it was truly as the World-Honored One had said, without any discrepancy.
The World-Honored One then addressed the bodhisattvas:
"You should practice the Dharma exactly as Mañjuśrī has done."
The assembly of bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison, saying:
"We shall indeed receive these instructions; we shall study the original practices of Mañjuśrī’s initial resolve, and we dare not be indolent or negligent in accomplishing this pure adornment."

At that moment, the World-Honored One smiled with joy; light issued from his mouth, brilliant in five colors, illuminating the ten directions and eclipsing the sun and moon. It circled his body three times and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; this smile must surely have a purpose.
By what causes and conditions was it prompted? I pray that the Buddha will explain it!"
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!

When the Buddha previously preached the Dharma and manifested the power of samādhi, everyone saw the Buddha-land of Universal Radiance in the eastern direction, fully endowed with all pure and majestic merits. The assembly was filled with joy and vowed to study it with resolve. Now, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas have all together resolved their minds to achieve such a pure and majestic land. Furthermore, there are eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas and sixteen virtuous men who have given rise to a heart of benevolence and compassion; they are gentle and refined by nature, and their aspirations are fulfilled. Such as these shall eventually attain the level of Mañjuśrī.”

The other bodhisattvas were not able to do as he did; nevertheless, by virtue of these merits and blessings, they will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to become most perfectly awakened ones, yet their accomplishment of a buddha-field will not equal the merit of Mañjuśrī’s adornment and purification.
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!

If there is a bodhisattva whose mind-nature is supremely true, who proclaims vows with their mouth without transgressing their original resolve, they shall likewise become fully endowed with a body like that of Mañjuśrī. Even if their mind is timid and weak, yet possesses faith and joy, by virtue of courageously proclaiming words of vow with their mouth, they shall further transcend the hardships of the beginning and end of sixty trillion *koṭis* of kalpas, and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) will thereby be fulfilled.”

At that time, the four bodhisattvas each manifested from their respective directions a multi-storied pavilion adorned with various precious jewels. Accompanied by hundreds of thousands of countless devas, they rained down celestial flowers and played manifold musical instruments. Through the majestic transformations of their supernormal powers, the earth shook and trembled. They approached the World-Honored One from the four directions together; as their light illuminated the assembly, all who saw it were filled with joy.
Maitreya knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now the earth shakes greatly and celestial flowers fall in profusion; the multi-storied pavilion shines brilliantly as people arrive from the four quarters; drums and music, stringed songs, and heavenly incense fill the air with fragrance—what auspicious omen is this?"
"By whose majestic power?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"

These four bodhisattvas immediately came to see the Buddha; employing their own supernormal powers to move the assembled multitude, they manifested these auspicious signs to exhort and transform them in the Dharma.
At that time, the four bodhisattvas approached the Buddha, prostrated themselves at his feet, and circumambulated him three times. The Buddha bade them sit, and they withdrew to take their seats.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas gathered in the assembly:
"These four upright gentlemen have exhorted and inspired many; the vows they have established are beyond measure.

If sons of noble family should show humble reverence and yearning toward these upright gentlemen, their nets of doubt regarding the meaning of the Dharma will be forever severed through inquiry. By practicing the bodhisattva deeds and eliminating the cycle of beginning and end, they will surely attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, transcending twenty billion kalpas of wandering affliction, and universally perfecting all dharmas and the six perfections."
"If there be any woman who hears the name and title of this true man, she shall swiftly transform her female body and quickly realize perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his majestic spiritual power, and the entire assembly returned to its former state; that Buddha-land suddenly vanished from sight.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One! All dharmas are like illusions;

what is created by a magician arises and immediately perishes. The successive transformation of all dharmas is likewise so. That which neither arises nor perishes is called 'equality. Those who study equality will surely attain perfect enlightenment, and having attained perfect enlightenment, they shall deliver and liberate all beings."
The Bodhisattva Prajñottara asked Mañjuśrī,
“By what practice does a bodhisattva achieve perfect awakening? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Neither attaining nor losing—this is called perfect enlightenment.
Huishang asked again:
"Is it possible to further attain that which cannot be attained?"
"Is it also non-existent?
If one does not attain existence, then there is no multitude that cannot be attained. Mañjuśrī replied:

"It is neither attainable nor non-existent. The reason it is not attainable is that these dharmas have all transcended arising; from the very beginning they have been non-existent, and they are not something that will come to be, nor can they be conceived as being attained."
Mañjuśrī further asked Hui-shang:
"What is the single practice for expounding the Dharma of the sutras?
Thereupon, Hui-shang replied:
"That which is neither produced nor destroyed, and does not create a separate dwelling—this is called the exposition of the sūtra-dharma through a single karmic act.
Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī said:
"That which neither comes nor goes—this is called the exposition of the sūtra-dharma through a single karmic act."
The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said:

"That which is without attainment and without equality, which neither realizes nor is tranquil, and which is without dullness or fear and without past, future, or present—this is called the single practice of expounding the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Yiyuan said:

"To not falsely conceptualize the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; to not dwell upon bodhisattvas; to have no notion of a land and no thought of hell; to not sever phrases and sentences, and to not rely on permanence—this is called the single practice of expounding the sūtras and the Dharma."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:

"Not perceiving the five aggregates or the various elements of the sense bases; not seeing yet not being blind, free from false conceptualizations; not entering into phenomena, neither accumulating nor abandoning—this is called the single practice of expounding the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Lion-Gait-Thunder-Voice said:

"That which is undisturbed amidst chaotic dharmas, which does not construct various things as being the dharmas of ordinary persons, but regards this training in the Dharma as the dharmas of all Buddhas; which harbors no deluded thoughts and does not grasp at a single dharma; whose activity is tranquil—this is called the single activity of expounding the sūtra-dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:

"To realize that which is fundamentally non-existent and not to conceive of it as existing now—this profound and wondrous Dharma is entirely free from delusive thoughts; this is called the single practice of expounding the sutras and the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Unhindered Eloquence said:

"When all dharmas are exhausted and have reached ultimate exhaustion, this is called 'inexhaustible. To expound all dharmas as being inexhaustible is what is meant by the single karmic activity of proclaiming the sūtra-dharma."
The Bodhisattva Śubhamatiman said:

"To have no thoughts regarding any mental objects, yet to enter into them without being without mind, neither gaining nor losing—this is called the single practice of expounding the sūtras and the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Awakening Beyond Dust said:

"To be unstained by any phenomena of the sensory realms, yet not being unstained either; neither clinging nor grieving; neither forgetting nor recollecting; neither acting nor non-acting; neither grasping nor abandoning—this is called the single practice of expounding the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Seabed said:

"His resolve is like the ocean, forever difficult to reach its bottom; he penetrates deeply into the essential points of the Dharma without perceiving false conceptualizations. He proclaims the Dharma according to what should be practiced, without 'self' and without 'other. This is called the single practice of expounding the sutras and the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Daśacandravimala said:
"When one regards all sentient beings as equal to the full moon, and the mind perceives no equality nor anything to be equalized—this is called the single activity of expounding the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Eliminating All Darkness of Sorrow said:

"To be able to bring rest to all the sores of sorrow, neither grieving nor being dejected; to be able to cut away the various roots of worldly confusion—what are these roots? They are the roots of the self (*ātman*). When there are those who preach the Dharma in accordance with the equal sutras and my own practice, this is called the single activity of expounding the teachings of the sutras."
The Bodhisattva Hook-Chain said:

"If one speaks of the Dharma without relying upon or clinging to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; without being attached to the teachings of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and without longing for the path of the Buddha—this is called the single practice of expounding the sutras and the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation said:

"To proclaim all dharmas equally as being identical to emptiness and non-existence, yet not dwelling on emptiness nor grasping at equality—when one speaks thus, this is called the single karmic activity of expounding the sūtras and the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Pure in the Three Grades said:
"When preaching the Dharma, one purifies the three grades of fields.
What are these three fields?"
Not grasping at a self, not conceptualizing assemblies of dharmas, and not relying on any phenomena—this is called the pure karma of the three spheres for proclaiming the teachings of the Dharma.
To speak in such a manner is called the single karma of expounding the sutras and the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Zaisuji said:

"To know that all dharmas return to equality, and having clearly understood this, to make distinctions without proclaiming words—because no dharma whatsoever is proclaimed—this is called the single activity of expounding the sutras and the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Gambhīracaryā said:
"If one perceives all phenomena yet perceives nothing at all, and speaks such words as these, this is called the single activity of expounding the Dharma."

In this manner, all the bodhisattvas each declared their aspirations. While this *Ekakarmika-sūtra* was being preached, seven thousand *koṭis* of bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eight hundred and forty-four million people all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; seven thousand bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind; and for ninety-six *nayutas* of devas and worldlings, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye arose.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Lion-Gait Thunder-Sound addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When Mañjuśrī attains Buddhahood as the Buddha Universal Manifestation, how many bodhisattvas will there be?"
"How long will his lifespan last, and when will he attain Buddhahood?
The Buddha said, "You should ask Mañjuśrī yourself; it shall be as the Buddha has instructed."
He asked Mañjuśrī, “Virtuous One, how long will it be before you attain supreme perfect enlightenment? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If space were to have form, then one would attain perfect enlightenment; if even a phantom person could achieve the Way of Buddhahood, then my body would likewise be free from attachment, with outflows extinguished, and I would attain supreme perfect enlightenment."

If there is a call, there is an echo; if there is a form, there is a shadow. When the moon can brighten the day and illuminate the night, only then shall my body achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
Those who aspire to seek the Way should inquire about the timing of their attainment of Buddhahood.
He asked again:
"Virtuous one, do you not aspire to seek the Way? He replied:
"No," he replied. [The other] asked:
"For what reason?"
He replied: "The Way is Mañjuśrī; Mañjuśrī is the Way. Why is this so?"
"It is merely a provisional designation.
Mañjuśrī and the Way—these names are quiescent; they are utterly devoid of conceptual understanding, for emptiness is what is called the Way.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhagāminigarjitasvara, saying:
“Have you ever seen or heard of the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the land of Amitāyus Buddha?
He replied, “Indeed, I have.”
"I have both seen and heard it.
The Buddha asked, "How much is there?"
He replied, "It is inconceivable and cannot be measured.
The Buddha said:

“The number of bodhisattvas who universally manifest in the Buddha-lands is comparable to the accumulation of dust filling the worlds of the ten directions; by comparison, the number of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of Amitāyus Buddha is like a single grain of dust.”
Furthermore, the lifespan of the Buddha Samantadarśin is infinite.

To provide an analogy: suppose one were to shatter all the three-thousandfold world systems of the ten directions into dust, scatter this dust beyond a thousand buddha-fields, and then place a single grain of dust at every point throughout the ten directions until all the dust was exhausted—O son of good family, would you be able to calculate or know the number of these grains of dust?
He replied, “There is no one who can limit it.
The Buddha said:

"The lifespan of the Tathāgata Universal Manifestation is equivalent to but a single mote of dust; even the analogy of motes of dust is insufficient to describe it. To understand its essential point: it is as boundless as space, such that years, lifespans, and kalpas cannot serve as a comparison."
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there should be someone who studies the Mahāyāna for the sake of this great wisdom and boundless insight, they ought to endure hardships through incalculable kalpas, taking refuge in and universally practicing the dharma of a bodhisattva; such a Great Way must not be neglected or abandoned."
The Buddha said: "So it is, Maitreya!
It is exactly as you have said."
Who, upon hearing of this infinite great wisdom, would not resolve their minds on the Way and take delight in it?
Only those of indolent and petty character, who do not understand the true and correct, fail to find joy in it.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, ten thousand people gave rise to the mind of the Great Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Lion-Gait Thunder-Sound, saying:

"Now, in praising Mañjuśrī’s own past conduct and his original vows, he has delivered immeasurable Buddhas and countless bodhisattvas. His wisdom of the Way and his sublime virtues are inconceivable; even all those who have attained the Way throughout the ten directions cannot exhaustively describe them through metaphors."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there were someone who established great vows and the practice of the infinite, would their aspirations be equal to those of Mañjuśrī?"
"Enduring diligent ascetic practices, one remains without weariness or fatigue throughout incalculable eons, never giving rise to thoughts of exhaustion.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!"
"What is your intention?
Does space ever think, 'I am traveling through days and nights, months and years, seasons, limits of time, or kalpas'? He replied:
"No," he replied. [The Buddha] said:
"In this way, son of good family!"

One clearly understands that all phenomena are also like space; as space is quiescent and stable, it does not conceive of day or night, sun or moon, seasons, years, or the duration of kalpas. Why is this so?
In emptiness, there is no thought or reflection; how could there be any notion of exertion?

Even through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is neither increase nor decrease; it does not decline, nor does it flourish; it is not destroyed, nor is it ruined; it is neither born nor aged; it is neither sick nor dead; it neither departs nor arrives.
Why is this so? Because emptiness and existence are merely provisional designations!

Mañjuśrī’s name is likewise; one who can understand it as being like empty space will fully know that all dharmas are entirely without words and utterly non-existent, and thus shall have no fear and no weariness.
“Mañjuśrī has long since attained Buddhahood; such is his resolve, and it is the same for those who are equal to Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaragarbha said to Mañjuśrī:
“The great vows you have undertaken are beyond comparison; if there are those who study, how should they advance?”

Mañjuśrī replied: "If there are those who would learn my armor of great vows, their aspiration for those vows should be like an illusion or a transformation; thus, there is nothing that exists, nor is there anything to be done."

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Devānām Indra, and other honored, great, and wondrous deities all raised their voices in unison and together exclaimed:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"

To hear this sutra is to obtain excellent benefit and boundless joy; how much more so for those who receive, uphold, recite, and study it! I shall receive, uphold, recite, and study it, and I shall explain it extensively for others, causing it to spread everywhere, protecting its practitioners so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Then, the Bodhisattva Siṃhakramavijitagarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
If there are those who receive, uphold, recite, and chant this sutra, what blessings and merit shall they obtain?"
“If there are those who hear this and immediately resolve their minds to pursue and study it, what then shall be the model for Mañjuśrī?

The Buddha said, “If there are bodhisattvas who study this Dharma, they will be like the Tathāgata, free from all obstructions. Suppose that in the final age of the future, one were to fill the buddha-fields of the ten directions with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift to the Buddhas to make offerings to them all; suppose one maintained an impartial mind toward all sentient beings without ceasing throughout kalpas; and furthermore, suppose one combined the giving of the Dharma, fully possessing the six perfections—this merit would still not be worth calculating. It would not equal the merit of hearing this sublime and pure sutra-dharma and resolving to study it with longing.”
Mañjuśrī! If one recites and chants [the name] while walking within seven paces, the merit thereof exceeds that by hundreds of billions of times; it is beyond analogy and cannot be calculated.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what name should this sutra be upheld?
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"This sutra is titled 'The Extraordinary Fulfillment of Desires and Delights'; you should uphold it!

It is also titled 'The Meritorious Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field,' and it is further titled 'The Joyful Resolve of Those Who Generate the Mind of Enlightenment'; you should firmly maintain it!"

At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions all scattered celestial flowers as an offering to this Dharma, and they extolled the immeasurable virtues of Mañjuśrī. The moisture of the Dharma universally nourishes and its vast protection covers the three realms; those who open their hearts and receive it shall all attain perfect enlightenment. They then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and suddenly vanished, each returning to their own land.

When the Buddha spoke these words, as many bodhisattvas as there are sands in the Ganges River attained the stage of non-retrogression, believing that these bodhisattvas were fully endowed with the roots of virtue.
At that time, Mañjuśrī entered a samādhi called "Universal Illumination of Light and Words Taught as Illusory," and through the concentration of this mind, he entered right meditative absorption.

Having entered this samādhi, the entire assembly saw Mañjuśrī appearing universally before each and every Buddha in incalculable Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, standing before those Buddhas and extolling the virtues of the purity and adornment of his own land.
Having seen this, the assembly marveled at what had never before occurred, exclaiming:

"The vows of Mañjuśrī are inexhaustible; his virtue and wisdom are lofty and transcendent, beyond compare. He causes his body to manifest throughout the ten directions, yet remains seated here without moving; his majestic spiritual power and merit are magnificent and irreproachable."

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the assembly of bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world, were all greatly rejoiced. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid their respects, and departed.
The Sutra on the Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field, Scroll II.
